screens.body:
Analysis asks "WHAT must the system do?" Design asks "HOW will we build it?" It's the bridge between requirements and code — the decisions you make before anyone types a line.

Skipping design and jumping to code feels fast. It's actually the slowest route: every design decision you postpone becomes a rewrite later, when changing things costs ten times more.

options: Deciding HOW the system will be built, before coding
Writing the code as fast as possible
Testing the finished product
check.question: System design is…

screens.heading: From what to how
screens.keyPoint: Design is deciding how, before building.

screens.body:
A class diagram is the blueprint of your code's structure. Each class is a box with three sections: the name (Task), the attributes — the data it holds (title, budget, status), and the methods — what it can do (publish(), assign()).

Here's the lovely part: the classes usually fall right out of your requirements. The nouns in your use cases — task, user, payment — become classes. Analysis hands design a vocabulary; design organizes it.

options: Boxes showing each class's name, attributes, and methods
A drawing of the user interface
A list of bugs
check.question: A class diagram shows…

screens.heading: Class diagrams
screens.keyPoint: Nouns become classes; verbs become methods.

screens.body:
Classes don't live alone — the lines between them are relationships. Association is the plain one: a User "posts" a Task. Inheritance is the family one: an Admin "is a" User with extra powers. Aggregation is the parts one: an Order "has" OrderItems.

Getting relationships right matters because code copies the diagram. Wrong relationship on paper becomes wrong structure in code — and wrong structure is the hardest thing to refactor later.

options: How classes connect: association, inheritance, aggregation
How fast classes run
The order classes were written in
check.question: Relationships describe…

screens.heading: How classes connect
screens.keyPoint: Draw the lines carefully — code will copy them.

screens.body:
Three big OOP ideas, simply: inheritance means a class reuses and extends another (a "PremiumUser is a User"). Encapsulation means each class guards its own data — outsiders ask politely through methods instead of grabbing fields directly. Polymorphism means different classes can respond to the same message in their own way (every Payment type has a pay() method, each works differently).

You don't need to memorize textbook definitions. Just feel the pattern: reuse, protect, and "same message, different behavior."

options: Reuse (inheritance), protect data (encapsulation), same message different behavior (polymorphism)
Three kinds of loops
Three database types
check.question: Inheritance, encapsulation, polymorphism ≈

screens.body:
A data dictionary is the glossary for every piece of data in the system: each item's name, what it means, its type, and the rules for valid values. Example: status — "the task's current state" — text — must be one of: open, in-progress, completed, cancelled.

It also records cardinality and optionality — how many and whether required: "a task has exactly one poster" vs "a task may have many bids." Boring? Maybe. But it's the document that stops two developers from meaning different things by "status."

options: A glossary of every data item: meaning, type, valid values
A dictionary app
A list of passwords
check.question: A data dictionary is…

screens.heading: The data dictionary
screens.keyPoint: One shared meaning for every data item.

screens.body:
Two principles judge every design. High cohesion: each piece does ONE job well — a Payment class shouldn't also send emails. Low coupling: pieces depend on each other as little as possible — so changing one doesn't break five others.

The test is always the same: "if I change this, what else breaks?" Good designs answer "almost nothing." That's what makes software you can actually maintain instead of fear.

options: Each piece does one job (cohesion) and depends little on others (coupling)
As many features per class as possible
Classes that all depend on each other
check.question: Good design means…

screens.heading: What makes a design good
screens.keyPoint: One job per piece; few dependencies between pieces.

screens.body:
Architecture is design at the biggest scale: how the major parts are arranged. The layered style stacks them — presentation (screens), logic (rules), data (storage) — each layer only talking to the one below. Client-server splits work between the user's device and a central server (you know this one from web dev).

There's no perfect architecture, only tradeoffs. Pick the one whose strengths match your system's needs — and write down WHY, so future-you remembers the reasoning.

options: How the system's major parts are arranged (e.g. layered, client-server)
The building the team works in
A type of diagram software

screens.keyPoint: Arrange the big parts; document the why.
